content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper addresses the problem of test-time adaptation on video streams. It proposes new benchmarks, introduces a new dataset and further proposes a solution based on MAEs and a buffer of recent samples, where the model learn continuously (without resetting at every frame). Empirical and theoretical results support the proposed method, which performs better than several baselines on the tasks at hand.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Writing**

- Strengths. The paper is very well written, methodology and results are clearly exposed and related work shows good connections between recent and less recent trends. I appreciated the connections between the "test-time training" trend with the more classical online learning: while they differ in terms of assumptions, they are intimately related, but this has been overseen in some recent research papers.

**Contributions**

- Strengths. This work focuses on a very important topic, namely learning from data streams in an unsupervised fashion. To make a parallel with human learning, this is how humans learn for most of their time and it is in sharp contrast with the operating setting of most of learning algorithms used in computer vision (learning offline, from huge amount of labelled data).

- Weaknesses. The claim "all settings in continual learning have distinct splits of training and test sets" is not accurate: there is prior art focusing on the same problem (learning online, without human help, from data streams). Recently, (Volpi et al., CVPR 2022)  addresses this problem for the task of semantic segmentation (this work also explores the two scenarios detailed at the end of Section 3, referring to them as "naive" and "continual"). Before that, this problem has been addressed in the context of stereo and monocular depth estimation -- e.g., see (Tonioni et al., CVPR 2019a), (Tonioni et al., CVPR 2019b) for the former and (Zhang et al., CVPR 2020) for the latter

(Volpi et al., CVPR 2022): "On the Road to Online Adaptation for Semantic Image Segmentation"

(Tonioni et al., CVPR 2019a): "Learning to adapt for stereo"

(Tonioni et al., CVPR 2019b): "Real-time self-adaptive deep stereo"

(Zhang et al., CVPR 2020): "Online depth learning against forgetting in monocular video"

**Methodology**

- Strengths. The idea of having a buffer of recent samples instead of an episodic memory (like in standard continual learning) is reasonable and proved to be effective. Using MAE instead of other self-supervised learning algorithms is supported by recent results showing that this self-supervised learning technique allows learning very strong visual representations.

- Weaknesses.

1.  About adapting to single images: I think the point "while we can naively apply this to a video [...] this misses the point of using a video" is oversimplified. Using single images in videos instead of shuffled sample collection opens a range of possibilities to carry out research, e.g., on efficiency. For example, adapting on $1$ every $K$ frames: this makes sense using videos, since images are temporally correlated, but not on shuffled datasets, since samples are iid. This also relates to point 2 below.

2. According to Section 6, the proposed learning strategy is $200 \times$ slower than standard TTT. This makes the propsed strategy unusable on actual data streams, and it is a severe weakness since most of the applications in which one may desire to process data streams require low latency. What about leveraging the temporal correlation across frames and avoid learning at every time step? How would performance be affected? Given temporally dense sequences, there should be a sweet spot between accuracy and efficiency, by adapting every $K$ frames.

3. I could not find details about the training hyperparameters, neither in the main paper or in the Appendix. For example, I understand from Section 6 that the number of iterations is set to $100$, which is unusable in real applications; can the Authors expand on this, explaining which hyperparameter they tried for both their method and the baselines? Given the temporal consistency of the frames, I would assume that even setting the number of iterations to $1$ per frame should have an effect.

**Results**

- Strengths.

1. This paper proposes results on very important benchmarks, also introducing a new dataset. It is the first time test-time adaptation is assessed on tasks such as instance/panoptic segmentation and colorization.

2. TENT evaluated on new transformer-based architectures with LayerNorm.

- Weaknesses.

1. Lack of statistical analysis. How do results change across different video sequences? Reporting them as mean $\pm$ std will provide the reader with important information about which method is more reliable. Also, given the nature of the task, it would be nice to see some plots, showing how performance evolves throughout a video sequence. This would be easy to achieve, e.g. with a temporal window over the performance of the past $K$ frames. A single number summarizing performance across several videos leaves behind important information.

2. It would be nice to also have information related to computation/memory complexity of the different baselines/methods in tables, since the framework is well suited for practical applications. 

3. About the baselines, TENT results should be included also for the instance/panoptic experiment (Table 3). Furthermore, it should be tested both in the reset and in the non-reset settings. (Volpi et al., CVPR 2022), referenced above, showed that TENT with reset generally helps in online adaptation for semantic image segmentation, whereas -- without reset -- results can oscillate more (see N-TENT and C-TENT, respectively, in Table 1). 

4. (Minor) Another important baseline is self-training with pseudo-labels. Also in this case, results can change significantly according to whether reset is performed or not. This is labeled as "Minor", because prior art has already shown that TENT outperforms PL, hence, we can expect the same under these settings.

5. (Minor) Lack of metric to make conclusions on the video colorization experiment. If "quantitative metrics often misrepresent performance", a solution is to carry out a qualitative assessment showing results to different human subjects. We cannot take the Authors' word for "our method visually improves the quality of colorization in all the videos that we experimented with", and the reader should not necessarily access a website to draw their own conclusions. Figure 2 is promising, but it only contains a bunch of image results. 

**Other.**

Can the Authors clarify which results supports the claim in the introduction "forgetting can be beneficial instead of harmful"?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- **Clarity/quality**. The paper is very well written in general and results are clearly exposed.

- **Reproducibility**. The method is not reproducible because important hyperparameter are missing. The code is provided, but one should be able to understand and potentially implement the method without looking at it.

- **Novelty**. Using MAE with temporal buffer for test-time adaptation is novel. Furthermore, I had never seen before instance/panoptic segmentation and colorization tackled in a continual/online adaptation setting. As mentioned above, the Authors should tune down the claims about the novelty re: not using "distinct splits of training and test sets" in continual learning, since it is not a new framework.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I believe the test-time adaptation and online learning communities can benefit from this work. The problem of test-time adaptation in a streaming learning setting is currently under studied and this work proposes interesting benchmarks, as well as a possible solution.

On the other hand, the proposed methodology is extremely computationally intensive and the experimental analysis lack some important details about the implementation and the statistics of the results. Furthermore, some baselines are missing. 

I look forward reading the Author response and engaging in discussions.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper uses continuous model adaptation to improve the quality of video inference tasks. The paper uses self-supervised training for adapting the core feature extractor, but the final prediction head doesn't change over time. The authors released a dataset of 10 annotated videos with an average duration of 5 minutes.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The idea that adapting the feature extractor might be more important than the prediction head is interesting as it might remove the dependency on the ground-truth labels, which typically requires running an expensive "teacher" model for extracting those labels during the adaptation. However, intuitively, such a system shouldn't work robustly if the experiments run long enough to observe significant data drifts, given that the prediction head h is fixed and we're constantly varying the feature extractor f. The paper cites Sun et al. (2020) to justify this assumption, but I cannot understand how this can work in the face of strong input distribution shifts from the initial point. This could be empirically better justified on a longer video that relies on a huge state-of-the-art network for extracting the ground-truth labels. 

The bias-variance trade-off extracted in section 5.2 is very interesting indeed. However, as explained above, assumption 3 seems a bit unrealistic to me as $\delta_t$'s variance can generally grow with time as the head h gets outdated over time. 

As the paper mentions in the limitations, such a way of TTT requires 1600x more compute resources than a typical inference. A fair evaluation baseline that I didn't find was how would a 1600x larger generic model that is pre-trained on a very large corpus of data would do in this case. Given the prior work in this space, as I mention a few more next, taking into account the computation requirement of such adaptations plays a major role in interpreting the results.

The paper provides a good overview of the prior work in the ML community. However, it misses prior work in the Systems for ML community that try to address a similar problem [1, 2, 3] under keywords such as model adaptation, continuous learning, and drift recovery. I think it'd be really helpful to consider the compute requirements in evaluations as, for example, an object detection model also achieves variable accuracies given the compute budget.

[1] Khani, M., Hamadanian, P., Nasr-Esfahany, A. and Alizadeh, M., 2021. Real-time video inference on edge devices via adaptive model streaming. In Proceedings of the IEEE/CVF International Conference on Computer Vision (pp. 4572-4582).

[2] Bhardwaj, R., Xia, Z., Ananthanarayanan, G., Jiang, J., Shu, Y., Karianakis, N., Hsieh, K., Bahl, P. and Stoica, I., 2022. Ekya: Continuous learning of video analytics models on edge compute servers. In 19th USENIX Symposium on Networked Systems Design and Implementation (NSDI 22) (pp. 119-135).

[3] Suprem, A., Arulraj, J., Pu, C. and Ferreira, J., 2020. ODIN: automated drift detection and recovery in video analytics. Proceedings of the VLDB Endowment, 13(12), pp.2453-2465.
Vancouver
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This paper is well-written and provides good clarity into the assumptions of the work. The novelty could be much better communicated if the evaluation had taken into account the practical aspects of the problem, such as compute footprint and training delays. The approach of releasing a new video dataset of 10 manually annotated "videos" with an average length of 5 minutes can be very helpful for future work in this space. However, it might not be still long enough to support the claim that we can optimize the feature extractor independent of the prediction head.
content.summary_of_the_review:
I like the contribution of the paper, but not currently convinced with the practicality aspect of the evaluations.

Minor comment:
"This makes it possible for our “student” – the only model considered – to improve performance instead of efficiency."
First, performance and efficiency are vague wordings. But given the context, I assume you mean improving the task performance and compute efficiency. Second, these two are typically convertible to each other --if you get a better task performance at the same amount of resource consumption, then it usually means you consume less resources for the same task performance level.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
In this paper, the authors introduce a test-time training method for video tasks based on the masked autoencoder.
Additionally, the author released a new dataset--COCO videos, with 10 5-minutes videos. 
The proposed method outperforms the baseline model on 3 different tasks.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Pros:

(1) This paper can be seen as a pioneer work for video-based test-time training task. 

(2) This paper is well-written.


Cons:

(1) Low novelty: 
Compare to Gandelsman et al., (2022), the proposed method adds the sliding window strategy to apply to the video domain. In my view, we had better add more video-specific designs when we apply the image methods to the video domain. So I think the novelty of this paper is not enough.

(2) Missing the comparison with the test-time training methods. For most test-time training methods, we will compare with BN [1], TTT [2], and Tent, while the authors only compared with Tent on the KITTI-STEP dataset.


[1] Improving robustness against common corruptions by covariate shift adaptation. NeurIPS 2020

[2] Test-time training with self-supervision for generalization under distribution shifts. ICML 2020
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity: This paper is well-written.

Quality: The paper has minor technical flaws.

Novelty: The novelty of the proposed method is marginal

Reproducibility: The authors have provided the code in the supplemental materials.
content.summary_of_the_review: As mentioned in 'Strength and Weaknesses', the proposed method novelty is marginal and missing many comparison experiments. I tend to first give the rating of 'marginally below the acceptance threshold'.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper present a method of training a network on test samples without the labels -- so, learning the representation using test samples. On semantic segmentation and colorization problem, the proposed method outperforms baseline approaches. The authors also analyze the behavior of the proposed method in details in Sec. 5.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**
- S1: Early adaptation of the idea of TTT for video analysis.

**Weaknesses**
- W1: **No novelty** - The proposed method is an application of TTT to video.
- W2: **Heavy computational cost at the inference phase** - Like all TTT methods, this method also incurs significant amount of cost in the inference.
- W3: **Results are not compelling** - At the expense of heavy computational cost in inference time, the qualitative results (in the shared HTML) are not very compelling. (And there is no time complexity analysis)
- W4: **Overclaims** - The paper claims that forgetting can be beneficial for TTT. But there is no clear empirical or theoretical supporting evidence for this claim -- Figure in Sec. 5.1 indicates that Mean IoU trends on the windows size. Large windows size not only implies more forgetting but also incurs difficulty in learning due to challenging long-horizon encoding problem. Without factorizing the problem, the forgetting related claim is not well supported.
- W5: **Presentation is largely unclear** - There are numerous sentences that are not clear. It significantly harms the understanding of arguments. (Not complete) list of presentation improvements is found in the following "clarity, quality, novelty and reproducibility" section.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
**Presentation improvement suggestions**
- In Fig. 1, the colors for each class are different from frame t=270 and t=271. Thus, it is not easy to compare the results over time.
- Abstract is hard to follow due to numerous grammatical errors and undefined concepts.
  - What is "visual generalization"?
  - What is "independent images"?
  - What is "soothly changing environment"?
  - What is the "natural agents" referring to?
- Some of the citations have outdated venues. To name a few...
  - He et al.'s "Masked Autoencoders Are Scalable Vision Learners" has been published in CVPR 2022 proceedings not an arxiv entry.
  - Cheng et al.'s "Masked- attention mask transformer for universal image segmentation." has been published in CVPR 2022 proceedings not an arxiv entry.
  - Banerjee et al.'s "Self-Supervised Test-Time Learning for Reading Comprehension" has been published in NAACL 2021 proceedings not an arxiv entry.
content.summary_of_the_review: By unclear description, overclaims, little novelty and heavy computation requirement, the reviewer recommend to revise and resubmit to other venue.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.
